newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon finds presidential aircraft safe. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Pentagon finds presidential aircraft safe. [CORRECTED 22:50 GMT]

text.p: The Pentagon gave a clean bill of health on Tuesday to the aircraft fleet that ferries the president and other U.S. leaders despite recent mishaps.

A study conducted at White House request found that presidential airlift operations had been "virtually flawless" while executive support air fleet overall was being operated "safely and reliably," the Pentagon said.

The White House requested the study after an August 17 crash in Wyoming of a C-130 cargo plane that accompanied President Bill Clinton on vacation, and a September 6 crash involving presidential support helicopters in Florida.

"The Department of Defence review of Air Force and Marine Corps executive air support has found that the Department operates its executive support air fleet safely and reliably," the Pentagon said in a statement.

But retired Navy Vice Admiral Donald Engen (corrects spelling), a former Federal Aviation Administration head who led the Pentagon review, urged the White House to "critically review" the use of aircraft not permanently dedicated to serving the president.
He said Air Force and Marine Corps aircraft dedicated to the president maintain "high degrees of safety" when compared to civil fleets and other military aircraft fleets.
"The degree of safety is not as high once Executive airlift is passed to general support airlift forces in the field," Engen reported.

"This is not to say that this is unsafe; it is not. But, different training, operations, maintenance and experience criteria apply in those combat-related and combat-support organisations designed to fight wars," Engen said.
On Monday, the Air Force blamed crew error in the Wyoming crash, in which the four-engine aircraft slammed into a mountain near Jackson Hole.
